491529b910b049ec.text: Every text has a job. A text is anything made to share a message: a recipe, a job ad, a group chat, a film, a safety sign. Each text type has a job, and its job decides its shape. Informative texts give facts: news reports, notices, workplace reports. Look for headlines, dates and plain, factual words. Persuasive texts want you to think or do something: ads, opinion pieces, posts. Look for strong words, pictures and a call to action. Instructional texts tell you how: recipes, manuals, safety procedures. Look for numbered steps, lists and “doing” words (mix, press, wear). Narrative texts tell a story: films, novels, a mate's story about the weekend. Look for characters, a problem and an ending. Many everyday texts mix types. An email might inform and persuade. A job ad informs you about the job, then persuades you to apply. To work out any text, ask: What's its job? Who's it for? How is it set out? What kind of words does it use?

0834ed8ff6addf20.text: One storm, many texts. The Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) is Australia's weather agency. When a storm is coming, it doesn't write just one text. It shares the same news in different text types, for different jobs and readers. A forecast on its website and app gives facts: heat, rain and wind, set out by day. A warning is put out when the weather could be dangerous. It's short and urgent. It says what's happening, where, and what to do. Social media posts share the key message fast, often with a map or video. They're for people scrolling on their phones. Same weather. Different jobs, different readers, different shapes. Think about it. What's the job of a forecast? Of a warning? Why would a warning be short and urgent? Who reads BoM's social media posts, and how is that different?

Every text type is built for a purpose and audience, with its own structure and features. Recognising them lets you read faster, judge whether a text works, and choose the right type when you write. By the end you can: I can name common text types and what each one is for. I can spot the structure and features of a text. I can compare two text types. I can choose the right text type for a job.
